text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Leaders of the influential metalworkers' and local authority workers' unions, along with the Federation of Swedish Industry, jointly spoke out in favour of retaining nuclear power. The three urged a review of the policy whereby some reactors will be mothballed before the end of their working life for environmental reasons.

- An investor organisation, IR-Foreningen, will propose next January that companies make public their profits forecasts, rather than restricting the information to analysts. Firms should at least invite representatives of the electronic media to forecast sessions, IR chairwoman Inger Larsson said.

- The government speaks with a forked tongue over the need for a budget surplus, the paper said. Finance Minister Erik Asbrink insists in Sweden that a surplus is necessary if Sweden wants to exercise the option to remain outside Economic and Monetary Union. Abroad, however, Sweden argues that budget surpluses are a precondition for all countries which do want to join EMU.

- A former member of law firm Lagerlof & Leman has been arrested on charges of infringing tax law and other offences. The man, who was not named, was a leading authority on competition law, and left the law firm after an internal investigation showed he had broken internal rules.

- Sweden now has 50 days until the end of 1996 in which to decide if it will enter the exchange rate mechanism as a prelude to Economic and Monetary Union by January 1, 1999. The Riksbank wants to link the crown to European currencies while the government has so far kept a low profile so as not to inflame political differences.

- The Nordic region is growing faster than EU countries as a whole, Swedbank chief economist Hubert Fromlet said in a report presented on Monday. Taking Baltic littoral states as a group, he said Poland had the highest economic growth, put at five percent this year and 5.5 percent in 1997.

- MoDo's management is due to decide next autumn whether or not to scrap its pulp plant at Domsjo after 93 years of operation. Such a move would deprive the Ornsjoldsvik area of a further 400 jobs and is likely to be fiercely contested by local managers and unions.
